cards.artisan: Mike Taylor and John Hatfield came off the Nike payroll on a Friday in February 2017 and opened Artisan the following Monday, in the same ten-thousand-square-foot shop Nike had used to build golf clubs. Taylor was Nike’s model maker for irons and wedges and Hatfield built putters. Taylor still grinds every wedge himself, and you cannot order one without coming to Fort Worth to be fitted.
cards.p53: Christopher Griffin left Microsoft in 2012 to build P53, named for Ben Hogan’s 1953 season, the year he won three of the four. The shop leases space at Leonard Golf Links — the old Nike building — from Marty Leonard, whose father founded Colonial. Every iron starts as a single billet of certified American steel, struck at around 2,100°F under a gravity hammer, then machined, ground and finished in house. Admission is by invitation only.
cards.piretti: Mike Johnson designs every Piretti head, and every one is milled from a solid billet — there has never been a cast putter in the line. Two specs set him against the rest of the industry: heads run fifteen to forty-five grams heavier than standard, and loft is set at 2.5 degrees because greens are cut shorter than they used to be. It is all made in a shop on Stuebner Airline Road north of Houston.
cards.edison: Terry Koehler has been designing wedges longer than most brands have existed: EIDOLON, which put the first CNC-milled grooves in a production wedge, then SCOR, then the Ben Hogan relaunch. Edison is the distillation of all of it, and the patented Koehler Sole puts high and low bounce in the same head so one wedge covers more lies. In 2021 he moved design, assembly and shipping to the Gulf Coast at Rockport.
cards.edel: David Edel built the brand on the idea that a putter should be fitted like a set of irons, because head shape, shaft lean and sightline all change where you aim before you have moved a muscle. The Brick is milled in the USA from premium stainless and hand-finished in Austin; the E-T01 is machined from carbon steel, then hand-painted, polished and assembled in Austin. Each head is finished individually by their own craftsmen.
cards.lamb: Tyson Lamb started in his mother’s garage north of Dallas, and the shop in Plano still runs on six employees. Their own description is the least romantic and the most accurate: a family owned Texas based machine shop. Putters are the headline and the engraving is the signature, turning up on ball markers, divot tools and the leather.
cards.criquet: Hobson Brown and Billy Nachman started Criquet in Austin in 2010, and the Players Shirt is still the whole argument: a soft, unfussy, slightly retro polo for anyone who did not want to dress like a tour caddie. The Top-Shelf runs 92 percent Pima cotton with removable collar stays. Criquet designs at the Clubhouse in Austin and has the shirts made in Peru, and prints that on the product page.
cards.olydoe: Scott Matthews left investment banking in New York because no cotton polo he wanted to play golf in existed, moved to Dallas, and started Olydoe on what he calls an anti-polyester manifesto. Everything is Supima cotton with hollow-core yarn, the performance without the plastic hand. The star in the logo is two stars, one from the Chicago flag and one from the Texas flag — a nine-hole course in rural Illinois, then Chicago, then Dallas.
cards.sierramadre: Bonny Riddle and Michelle Anderson make women’s golf clothing and play the game themselves, which shows in the details rather than the silhouettes: built-in bras, pockets that hold something, an elastic loop on the All Square Skort for a glove. The skort is Peruvian cotton and the Bad Madres bucket hat has its patch hand-stitched on in Austin. Select Golf Galaxy stores now carry them, which for a six-year-old brand is a real signal.
cards.juniperjames: James Elledge named Juniper & James after his twin daughter and son, and built it on what he learned starting Duck Camp, the Texas hunting and fishing label — specifically, how breathable fabric is supposed to work. The Comfort Polo is 48 percent Lenzing micro modal and 47 percent polyester, cut with a spread dress collar and mother-of-pearl buttons. Landa Park, Kissing Tree and The Quarry are the home courses listed on the site.
cards.kingfisher: Fiona Cohen was an art director at PepsiCo, and Kingfisher started at her kitchen counter in East Dallas with a sewing machine and thrift-store fabric. The brand sits in the overlap between her design background and her brother’s golf habit, and by their own admission it has not reached a pro shop yet. They ran a Worst Golfer in Dallas contest and signed the winner as their first sponsored athlete, which tells you the tone.
cards.bestgrips: Harry and Zach make leather grips in Conroe, a father-and-son shop. Harry’s father Bud took up golf while recovering from losing a leg in a plane crash, and the two of them ran the East Texas Amputee Golf Tournament. The line runs from the extra-tacky MicroPerf to Horween Dublin leathers with custom stitch colours, and the shop takes no minimum order and no paid endorsements.
cards.chipp: Randall Pulfer and Tyler Lane met as roommates at Wisconsin–Madison, asked why golf gloves are so boring, and started answering it in Dallas during the pandemic. The gloves are premium cabretta leather, perforated on both sides of every finger, with a reinforced palm. Ten percent of every glove goes to a charitable partner and many of the designs are drawn from that partner’s mission, starting with Feelin’ Lucky and Texas Hole’em.
cards.clintorms: Clint Orms began engraving in Dallas in 1992 and works now from a showroom on Water Street in Kerrville, with the bench still out in Ingram. He started out polishing for the sculptor and saddle maker Buck Brumley, then apprenticed under four silver designers across the West. His buckles are named for Texas counties — Bexar, Pecos, Duval — and he will not reproduce more than ten pieces from any one design. Ben Crenshaw is a client.
cards.knitty: Maggie knits headcovers one at a time, and the reason she knows how is that her mother taught her. The first set she made was a Father’s Day present for her golf-loving father in University of Maryland colours. What she sells now is the retro striped driver-and-fairway kind with a tassel or a pom on top, sets of three at around ninety-five dollars and putter covers at thirty-five.
cards.allyaiken: Ally Aiken is a watercolour artist and graphic designer in Austin whose older sister gave her a watercolour set and calligraphy tools one Christmas. She painted her first golf course map in 2020 as a gift for her husband Campbell and has not stopped since. The catalogue now runs to hundreds of courses, including Roy Kizer and Onion Creek in Austin and Brook Hollow and Dallas Athletic Club up in Dallas.

kickers.1: Texas builds golf clubs for an unromantic reason: when Nike left the equipment business in 2016 it left behind a building in Fort Worth and a group of people who knew how to grind a wedge. A named person touches every club before it ships.
kickers.2: Golf apparel is the easiest category to start a brand in and the hardest to stay in, which is why the span runs from Criquet in 2010 to Juniper & James last summer. Most are designed in Texas and sewn somewhere else, and the good ones say so on the product page.
kickers.3: These are the parts of the game you actually hold, and two of the three are hand-work in the literal sense — a silversmith engraving a marker, a father and son wrapping a grip. All three are small enough that an order goes past a person rather than a system.
kickers.4: Two people make things by hand and sell them, which is a different business from running a brand. Both started with a gift for a family member, which is how a surprising amount of this ends up beginning.
